title: U.S. Supreme Court rejects new trial in fatal Prince George’s County shooting
summary: A federal appeals court was wrong when it ordered a new trial for Jeremiah Antoine Sweeney, who was convicted of second-degree murder for an April 2010 shooting in Prince George's County, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters November 24, 2025

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters November 24, 2025

A federal appeals court was wrong when it ordered a new trial for Jeremiah Antoine Sweeney, who was convicted of second-degree murder for an April 2010 shooting in Prince George’s County, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday.

In a unanimous, unsigned ruling, the justices reversed the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which the high court said had wrongly ruled for Sweeney based on a claim that he “never asserted” in his appeal.

The justices wrote that Sweeney made “one, and only one claim” in his appeal — that his attorney at his trial was ineffective. His attorney put on no witnesses or evidence, and failed to question jurors to see if they had been influenced by one juror who made an unauthorized visit to the crime scene.

“Instead of ruling on that claim, the Fourth Circuit devised a new one, based on a ‘combination of extraordinary failures from juror to judge to attorney,’” the high court said in its ruling. “The Fourth Circuit’s ‘radical transformation’ of Sweeney’s simple ineffective-assistance claim ‘departed so drastically from the principle of party presentation as to constitute an abuse of discretion.’”

The justices wrote in their brief, four-page ruling that “’the parties frame the issues for decision,’ while the court serves as ‘neutral arbiter of matters the parties present.’” It sent the case back to the circuit court with instructions to reconsider Sweeney’s ineffective assistance of counsel claim only, in light of the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, which severely limits relief on appeal.

The Maryland Office of the Attorney General, which represented Prince George’s County in the case, declined to comment Monday on the high court’s ruling.

Jo-Ann Tamila Sagar, listed as an attorney for Sweeney, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

A Prince George’s jury found Sweeney guilty in 2011 of second-degree murder, attempted murder and weapons violations in a 2010 shooting during an argument over stolen marijuana, that ended up killing a bystander 75 yards away. He was sentenced to two consecutive life terms, plus 30 years.

Sweeney’s state court appeals were rejected, and his first post-conviction appeal to the federal system — claiming ineffective assistance of counsel — was turned down at the district court level.

But a divided three-judge panel of the 4th Circuit disagreed in March, ruling that Sweeney deserved a new trial.

Circuit Judge Roger Gregory, in a 46-page opinion joined by Judge Terence W. Boyle, wrote that the case was built entirely on eyewitnesses who identified Sweeney “as the shooter — late at night, on a crowded street,” where “vantage point was an issue; light was an issue,” and a murder weapon was never found.

When Juror No. 4 went to inspect the crime scene on his own, and then joined deliberations with the rest of jury before the judge was alerted, it threatened Sweeney’s right “to a fair and impartial jury, reaching a verdict based solely on the evidence presented in the courtroom,” Gregory wrote. But he said Juror No. 4 was “just the tip of the iceberg.”

“Despite this, the judge allowed Juror No. 4 to return to the jury lounge with the other jurors for over an hour, with no instruction that they not deliberate,” according to the opinion. “After ultimately excusing Juror No. 4, the judge never instructed the remaining eleven jurors that they were not to consider anything Juror No. 4 had told them.”

“Judge and defense counsel both failed in their responsibilities. The trial court judge did not properly inquire into the jury taint” by Juror No. 4, he wrote, and Sweeney’s attorney “rendered representation far short of what is objectively reasonable.”

“The breakdown of the judicial process in this case – from juror to judge to attorney – deprived Sweeney of his constitutional rights, and he is therefore entitled to a new trial,” Gregory wrote.

But Judge A. Marvin Quattlebaum Jr., in a 50-page dissent, said that Sweeney raised only one claim in his appeal — not receiving competent representation at trial. Despite that, the majority “raises on its own, and then decides the case on, a totally different ground from what Sweeney argued to the state courts, to the district court or to us on appeal,” justifying its decision based on “the special circumstances” of Sweeney’s case.

“That alone is a problem. What’s the standard for this? It seems purely subjective. Like beauty, special  circumstances are in the eye of the beholder,” Quattlebaum wrote.

“We are not free to scour the record for issues that we think are important when the parties never raised them below and then dispense our subjective views of justice. That, however, is exactly what the majority does,” he wrote.
